questions.q: The main difference between explicit and tacit knowledge is that: *

o.t: Explicit knowledge can be codified using words, pictures or numbers, while elicit knowledge is personal and difficult to express like beliefs, insights, and experience.
Tacit knowledge can be codified using words, pictures or numbers, while explicit knowledge is personal and difficult to express like beliefs, insights, and experience.
Explicit knowledge can be shared using different management tools and techniques like networking, communities of practice and discussion of practice and discussion forums.
Tacit knowledge can be shared using different information management tools and techniques like lessons learned register, library service and information gathering.

questions.e: Explicit knowledge refers to knowledge that can be easily articulated, documented, and shared. It includes knowledge that can be codified in words, pictures, or numbers. Tacit knowledge, on the other hand, is more personal and harder to formalize. It includes insights, intuitions, and experiences that are difficult to express and share.

questions.q: Andy is a project manager for a software project. The scope of the project was approved by the customer and key stakeholders at the beginning of the project, but whenever the customer validates the deliverables, he comes up with new requirements that he would like to add into the product. Andy is working with the customer to find what requirements were missed in the planning stages of the project and how to plan better in the future. What is the best description of his project's current situation? *
questions.e: Scope creep refers to the uncontrolled expansion of project scope without adjustments to time, cost, and resources. It occurs when new requirements are added to the project without proper change control processes. In this case, Andy's project is experiencing scope creep because the customer keeps coming up with new requirements after the scope was initially approved.

questions.q: A customer inspection will be done within one week for a project deliverable. The project manager and the team notice a significant variance in one of the project delivrables which might lead to missing a key milestone and the customer might apply financial penalties. A project team member has recognized the root cause of the variance and it will need a minor correction to a configuration element. If this correction is done, the project will be back on track. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Ask the customer to postpone the inspection till corrective action is done.

questions.e: There is a significant variance, so a change request is required.

questions.q: A more experienced certified-PMP project manager tells the project manager of the new project to compile lessons learned in the lessons learned register and make them available for future projects. What is included in lessons learned register? *

o.t: All the plans used in the project.

questions.e: The lessons learned register is a document that captures the knowledge gained during the course of a project. It includes information such as variances and their causes, what went well, what could be improved, and any other insights that can help in future projects. This helps in preventing similar issues and repeating successful strategies in future projects. While work performance information and customer reports might provide useful data, the primary focus of the lessons learned register is on documenting experiences, including variances and their causes, to benefit future projects.

questions.q: A project manager is executing work but finds that team members are waiting for approvals, causing bottlenecks. What technique can help accelerate decision-making? *
questions.e: Delegation of authority speeds up execution by empowering team members to make decisions within their responsibilities.

questions.q: During executing a construction project to build a new hospital, it has been noticed that the workers don't finish the tasks early, however they use all the time allocated for each activity regardless of how long it actually takes to complete the activity. This behavior is an example of: *
questions.e: Parkinson's law states that "work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." This means that if more time is allocated for a task than is needed, the task will take the entire time allocated regardless of how long it actually takes to complete. In this scenario, the workers are taking all the time allocated for each activity, even if they could finish the tasks earlier, which is a clear example of Parkinson's law in action.

questions.q: During nondestructive testing at a construction site, it was discovered that certain components are failing workability tests. The project team has identified the root cause of these failures and proposed a solution. However, the project deadline is tight and the solution would require an increase in the budget. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Invite suppliers to submit bids for a lower-cost solution.
Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
Request additional funding from the project sponsor.
Update the risk management plan to include the solution.

questions.e: A budget change needs to go through formal change control, hence a change request to the CCB is required.

questions.q: During project execution, key stakeholders request a change to ensure that the final product will satisfy their requirements. Why should the project manager submit a change request? *

o.t: To record the requirements needed for the stakeholders' sign-off in order to update the issues log.
To ensure that the request is formally documented and incorporated according to the integrated change control process.
To provide justification for any impact the change might have on the project's budget or schedule.
To ensure stakeholder responsibility regarding potential impact of the change on project budget and schedule.

questions.e: Submitting a change request is essential to formally document and manage changes according to the project's integrated change control process. This ensures that the change is reviewed, assessed for its impact on scope, schedule, cost, and quality, and approved or rejected in an organized manner. This formal process helps maintain project control, prevent scope creep, and ensure that all changes are properly evaluated and incorporated into the project plan.

questions.q: A customer wants to add new features to the project deliverable. Before the project manager can begin work on these new features, what should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Document the list of additional features in an email to the customer as a notification that the team will start working on the new features.
Draft the change request in the appropriate format to seek approval from the change control board (CCB) and start working on the new features only after approval is given.
Notify the project sponsor that the customer wants to add new features and wait for their approval to work on these new features.
Consult a subject matter expert (SME) and start working on the new features after there are no further concerns raised.

questions.e: Before beginning work on any new features or changes to the project deliverable, the project manager must follow the formal change control process. This involves drafting a change request and submitting it to the Change Control Board (CCB) for approval. This ensures that the impact of the changes on the project's scope, schedule, budget, and quality is properly assessed and that the changes are formally documented and approved before implementation. This process helps prevent scope creep and ensures that all changes are managed in a controlled and systematic manner.

questions.q: A project manager is managing a project with a distributed team, fixed budget, and tight deadlines. Knowing that they’re adopting a predictive approach, what should the project manager do to avoid any scope creep and keep their team focused on delivering a product that meets requirements? *

o.t: Ask the project team to skip small requirements so that they can only focus on big and important ones
Ensure that all alterations to the scope are authorized through a formal process
Prevent stakeholders from directly interacting with the project team
Scope creep cannot be avoided in a predictive project, therefore the project manager should adopt an agile approach instead

questions.e: To avoid scope creep in a predictive project, it is essential to have a formal process for managing changes to the project scope. This ensures that any changes are properly reviewed, assessed for their impact on the project’s objectives, schedule, and budget, and approved by the appropriate stakeholders before implementation. This formal process helps maintain control over the project scope and keeps the team focused on delivering a product that meets the initially defined requirements. Skipping small requirements or preventing stakeholders from interacting with the team are not effective or advisable strategies. Adopting an agile approach is not necessary if the project is planned to be managed predictively.

questions.q: A team is working on multiple project tasks simultaneously, but progress is slow due to frequent context switching. What is the best technique to improve efficiency? *

o.t: Reduce Multitasking and Focus on One Task at a Time
Use Fast Tracking to Work in Parallel
Apply Resource Leveling to Balance Workloads
Increase Team Size to Improve Output

questions.e: Multitasking reduces efficiency due to cognitive load and context switching. Focusing on one task at a time improves quality and speed. Fast tracking (B) speeds up projects but does not reduce context switching. Resource leveling (C) helps workload balance but does not address multitasking directly. Increasing team size (D) does not necessarily improve efficiency.

questions.q: A development team collaboratively works on the same task at the same time using one workstation. What technique are they using? *
questions.e: Mobbing involves the whole team working together on a single task at one workstation. Swarming (B) refers to multiple people addressing the same issue but working separately. Pair programming (C) involves two developers, not an entire team. Fast tracking (D) speeds up project tasks but does not involve collaborative execution.

questions.q: When a high-priority issue arises, multiple team members temporarily stop their assigned tasks and focus collectively on resolving the issue. What technique is being used? *
questions.e: Swarming occurs when multiple team members work simultaneously on a critical issue until it is resolved. Mobbing (B) involves full-team collaboration but on a single task. Multitasking (C) involves handling multiple unrelated tasks. Timeboxing (D) sets a fixed time for a task but does not involve team realignment.

questions.q: In an Agile team, two developers work on the same piece of code together—one writing code and the other reviewing it in real-time. What technique is being used? *
questions.e: Pair programming involves two developers working on the same task, improving quality and reducing defects. Swarming (B) is a broader approach where multiple members work on one issue. Mobbing (C) involves the whole team collaborating. Fast tracking (D) is used for schedule compression.

questions.q: A team is assigned multiple tasks, but instead of focusing on completing one before starting another, they keep switching between tasks. This leads to delays and inefficiencies. What is this an example of? *
questions.e: Multitasking leads to inefficiency because of frequent context switching, reducing focus and productivity. Swarming (B) involves multiple people working on the same issue together. Mobbing (C) is extreme collaboration on a single task. Fast Tracking (D) overlaps tasks to accelerate project delivery.

questions.q: A project manager wants to improve efficiency in task execution by focusing on the most impactful activities. After analyzing task performance, they discover that 80% of delays are caused by just 20% of project activities. How should the project manager apply the Pareto Principle to optimize execution? *

o.t: Prioritize resolving the 20% of tasks causing most delays to improve overall project efficiency.
Assign equal effort to all tasks to ensure fair distribution of resources.
Focus on completing the easier 80% of tasks first to show quick progress.
Increase team size to handle all tasks simultaneously and reduce bottlenecks by 20%.

questions.e: The Pareto Principle (80/20 rule) states that 80% of results come from 20% of efforts. Focusing on fixing the most problematic 20% of tasks maximizes impact and improves efficiency. Assigning equal effort (B) ignores the principle of prioritization. Completing easier tasks first (C) does not resolve major delays. Increasing team size (D) does not necessarily solve execution inefficiencies.

questions.q: A project team is struggling to meet performance expectations. The project manager decides to introduce a system where real-time feedback is collected, and continuous improvements are implemented. What technique is being used? *
questions.e: Learning loops involve continuous feedback and iteration to refine execution.

questions.q: A project manager sets a strict deadline but does not provide additional resources. The team completes the work in the given time, but the quality is lower than expected. What principle explains this? *
questions.e: Timeboxing is when work is limited to a fixed timeframe, sometimes leading to lower quality if time is insufficient. Parkinson’s Law (A) explains task expansion. Student Syndrome (B) describes procrastination. Self-Protection (D) is about avoiding responsibility.

questions.q: A project team is working on multiple tasks at once, but progress is slow. The project manager suspects multitasking is causing inefficiencies. What is the best approach? *

o.t: Reduce work in progress and focus on fewer tasks at a time.
Increase team size to distribute work more effectively.
Use fast-tracking to complete multiple tasks in parallel.

questions.e: Multitasking reduces efficiency due to frequent context switching. Increasing team size (B) may not solve workflow inefficiencies. Fast-tracking (C) is for schedule compression, not multitasking issues. Overtime (D) leads to burnout without fixing the root cause.

questions.q: Midway through project execution, a project team identifies a more efficient way to complete a critical task. However, the new approach differs from the approved project plan. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Require the team to follow the original plan to maintain consistency.
Approve the change immediately since it improves efficiency.
Assess the change’s impact and submit a formal change request if beneficial.
Escalate the proposed change to senior management for review.

questions.e: Process improvements should be formally evaluated to avoid unintended risks. Forcing adherence to the original plan (A) may ignore beneficial innovations. Implementing changes without approval (B) violates project controls. Escalation (D) is unnecessary without an impact analysis.

questions.q: A project team is experiencing frequent delays due to waiting for approvals. What should the project manager do to improve execution efficiency? *

o.t: Increase the frequency of meetings with stakeholders to get approvals faster.
Delegate approval authority to team leads when possible.
Implement a stricter deadline for approvals.
Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.

questions.e: Empowering team leads speeds up decision-making without bottlenecks. More meetings (A) increase administrative burden. Stricter deadlines (C) may cause rushed or uninformed decisions. Escalation (D) should be a last resort.

questions.q: A senior stakeholder requests a major scope change during project execution. The project team is already at full capacity. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Accept the request and assign additional resources.
Inform the stakeholder that no changes can be made at this stage.
Evaluate the impact on schedule, cost, and resources before making a decision.
Escalate the request to the change control board immediately.

questions.e: Scope changes require formal impact analysis before approval or rejection. Accepting changes (A) without evaluating feasibility is risky. Rejecting outright (B) may harm stakeholder relationships. Escalating (D) is premature without an assessment.

questions.q: A project team applies an iterative approach where they review completed work, gather feedback, and use insights to improve future work cycles. What concept does this represent? *
questions.e: Learning Loops involve cycles of execution, feedback, and improvement, allowing teams to adapt and refine their approach over time. Kaizen (B) is the philosophy of continuous improvement but does not necessarily follow a loop structure. Sprint Retrospectives (C) are Agile-specific but a type of learning loop. Continuous Integration (D) is a development practice, not an improvement framework.

questions.q: A project team is making a critical design decision, but there is uncertainty about future regulatory changes that may impact their choice. To maximize flexibility, they decide to delay the decision until more information becomes available. What principle are they following? *
questions.e: Last Responsible Moment (LRM) is a Lean concept where teams defer irreversible decisions until they have the most relevant information. Rolling Wave Planning (B) focuses on planning details progressively but is not specific to decision-making. Change Control Process (C) manages approved changes but does not address decision timing. Just-in-Time Decision Making (D) is similar but lacks the structured decision delay approach of LRM.

questions.q: After a major project failure, an organization conducts a detailed lessons learned review. However, when a similar project is initiated a year later, the same mistakes are repeated. What should be done differently? *

o.t: Incorporate the lessons learned into training programs and standard operating procedures (SOPs).
Conduct a more detailed failure analysis to identify deeper root causes.
Assign the same project manager to ensure previous mistakes are avoided.
Make project managers accountable for reviewing past project failures before starting new ones.

questions.e: Lessons learned must be institutionalized through training and SOPs to prevent repeated mistakes. Conducting more analysis (B) is useful but does not ensure corrective action. Assigning the same project manager (C) does not guarantee systemic improvements. Making PMs accountable (D) helps but does not embed changes into processes.
